Indonesia Emas 2045

Rencana Pembangunan Jangka Panjang Nasional 2025-2045

Kementerian PPN/Bappenas · Enacted as UU No. 59 Tahun 2024 · Promulgated 13 September 2024 · Looks ahead to 2045 · Quantified: 5 headline targets, 45 indicators, 4 phases

Force when published: law Status today: in force Reviewed as of 17 Nov 2026 3 of 7 themes · 16 of 35 claims reviewed Next review: not set EN

Original: UU No. 59 Tahun 2024, with Lampiran (334 pp.), JDIH Kemenko Infrastruktur. The report is in Indonesian.

Then · 2017 · Paired on this page

Visi Indonesia 2045, Bappenas oration deck, 26 September 2017. The vision's first public version, superseded by the 2024 law. Its dated targets (high income by 2035; 6.5% growth in 2020–2025) are old enough to test, so they appear beside the law's in §5, §8, §9, and §14.

No longer in force

[GAP] No refresh cycle (proposed: after BPS's full-year 2026 release, 5 February 2027) and no Indonesian version of this page. [STRAIN] The spec has one report per page; the paired deck needs a slot in the header.

In one line

Indonesia's 2045 plan rests on 6–7% growth a year; two years in, growth runs at 5.1–5.5%, and two shocks it does not discuss have arrived.

At a glance

Indonesia Emas 2045 is the long-term plan Indonesia wrote into law in September 2024. It aims for high income by 2038–2041 and an advanced economy by the centenary in 2045. It expects growth of 6–7% a year, led by productivity, to carry five headline targets. Two years in, growth is 5.1–5.5%, below the plan's floor of 5.6%. The tax ratio fell in 2025, while a free-meals programme of about 1% of GDP was added. US tariffs and an oil-price spike, which the plan does not discuss, have arrived. Manufacturing's share of GDP has risen since 2022, the direction the plan needs. Most 2045 targets are too early to judge; the measures that rest on public finances are worth revisiting.

Three things to know

  1. Growth was 5.11% in 2025 and about 5.5% in the first three quarters of 2026, against the plan's floor of 5.6%. A 6% average to 2045 now needs 6.1% a year, faster than any decade since 1990. As of Nov 2026 · BPS [GAP] 2026 quarters via release pages and press; decade comparison from the reviewer's record. Verify at BPS
  2. The tax ratio fell to 9.31% of GDP in 2025, against the plan's 10.7–11.2% for that year and 18–20% by 2045. A free-meals programme of about 1% of GDP was added in 2026. As of Jan 2026 · Kemenkeu [GAP] Ratio computed by DDTC/Kontan; verify at Kemenkeu
  3. Two shocks the plan does not discuss arrived in its first two years: a 19% US tariff on most Indonesian goods, agreed in July 2025, and an oil-price spike in February–April 2026 that took Bank Indonesia's policy rate from 4.75% to 5.5% by June. As of Jun 2026 · Bank Indonesia See §10 [GAP] Carriers give 75 or 100 basis points; verify at BI

02 · How to read this page

A vision in force for two years: its goals are aims, not forecasts

This report is a vision. Its goals are the authors' aims for 2045, not forecasts. The plan is two years old, so most goals are too early to judge. This page tests what the plan assumed, and asks what has changed since it was written.

Where a figure is "behind", that describes the distance between the latest published number and the plan's own path for that year. It does not describe a government. Where a change is a "challenge" or an "opportunity", it is judged against the vision's own goals, not the reviewer's preferences.

Two readings are kept apart. A rating says what the evidence shows so far about a claim the plan makes. A pressure reading says which new conditions bear on that claim from here, whether or not the data has yet moved.

How a claim has fared so far
ReadingRegister termMeaning
HoldsConfirmedThe evidence matches what the plan expected.
Goes furtherStrengthenedThe variable has moved further in the direction the plan expected.
Holds in partWeakenedThe direction holds; the size or timing does not.
Not supported so farInvalidatedThe evidence so far runs against what the plan expected.
Not yet reviewedNot yet reviewedToo early to test, or not yet checked.
Where a target figure stands
PositionMeaning
AheadThe latest figure is more than 3% better than the plan's path for its year.
On pathWithin 3% of the path.
BehindMore than 3% worse than the path.
MetThe target has been reached.
No longer in forceA target of the superseded 2017 deck; last-known status shown.
What new conditions may mean from here
Pressure readingMeaning
Under pressureNew conditions push against the claim.
SupportedNew conditions run with it.
MixedBoth at once.
WatchSomething new may bear on it; not yet clear which way.
UntouchedNothing found that bears on it.

A dashed outline means "not yet in the data". Each chip on this page names its strongest change, linked to §10.

Ratings rest on official sources only: statistics offices, central banks, ministries, and international bodies. Think tanks give context. News reports never support a rating; where one carried an official figure, the page says "verify at source".

Part B · The report, then

03 · Why it was written

Written into law in 2024 to replace the 2005–2025 plan, as growth slowed
  • Who asked for it. The constitution and the planning law (UU 25/2004) require a long-term national plan every 20 years. The previous one, RPJPN 2005-2025, expired at the end of 2024.
  • Who wrote it. Kementerian PPN/Bappenas, the national planning ministry, drafted the annex. Parliament and the President enacted it as UU 59/2024.
  • The moment. Drafted in 2023 on data to 2022, after the COVID-19 recession of 2020 (−2.1%) and during the 2022 commodity windfall. The plan opens with a diagnosis: growth slowing by period (5.7% → 4.7% → 5.0%), falling productivity, early deindustrialisation, and too much regulation. Enacted in the last months of the Jokowi government; implemented from October 2024 by the Prabowo government.
  • How it was made. Led by Bappenas, with a national consultation (Musrenbangnas keynote, Bali, 22 May 2023) and the usual cascade into five-year and annual plans.

Diagnosis: UU No. 59 Tahun 2024, Lampiran, printed pp. 14–26

The 2017 deck. A scientific oration by the Minister of National Development Planning at Universitas Indonesia on 26 September 2017, building on President Jokowi's "Impian Indonesia 2015-2085".

[GAP] Who chose the name "Indonesia Emas" (the centenary of independence), the political sponsor, who was consulted, and the modelling behind the growth paths are not recorded. [STRAIN] "The moment" is assembled from the standing check and the register; there is no account of the parliamentary passage.

04 · The questions it explored

Four of its eight questions are still central; three are not yet reviewed

The plan is organised as eight missions answering a diagnosis of key issues. The eight questions below are the review's reading of that diagnosis.

Question the report set out to informStatus todayWhy
1. How can growth rise from about 5% to 6–7% and stay there for 20 years?Still centralGrowth was 5.11% in 2025 and about 5.5% in 2026 to Q3. Official readings put potential growth near 5% (§7.9).
2. Can productivity become the engine, in place of more labour and capital?Still centralProductivity growth was negative over 2010–2023 and positive in 2021–2023 (§7.2).
3. Can manufacturing's share of GDP be turned around?Changed shapeThe share has risen since 2022, from 18.3% to 19.07%. The question is now pace, and markets for the lead products (§9, §10).
4. How is the demographic window used before it closes?Not yet reviewedTheme not evidenced. The 2025 intercensal survey puts the dependency ratio one point above projection (X8).
5. Can the state pay for the plan?Still centralTax ratio 9.31% in 2025; deficit 2.92% of GDP; private finance about 28% of infrastructure need (§7.3, §7.11).
6. Can regulation and institutions deliver?Still centralThe stock of regulation has not visibly fallen; the corruption index was 34 in 2025, against 38 projected (§7.6).
7. Can emissions fall on the net-zero-2060 path while growth speeds up?Not yet reviewedTheme not evidenced. The second NDC (Oct 2025) sets a 2030 level above the plan's path (X9).
8. Can regional gaps narrow, with eastern Indonesia's share rising?Not yet reviewedTheme not evidenced. The RPJMN's 2029 figure for eastern Indonesia is 22.4%, against 23.3% on the vision's path.

Questions that have emerged since. How does the plan absorb shocks it does not model, such as tariffs and energy prices? What do large new programmes (free meals, village cooperatives) and a new state investment holding (Danantara) mean for its finance? Does generative AI change the plan's "40% of jobs" view of technology?

[TRIAL] The eight questions and every status are new judgements; the plan states missions, not questions.

05 · The futures it set out

One goal at two speeds: high income by 2038 or by 2041

The plan sets one destination and two paths to it. A slower path, near or below 5% growth, is drawn as the warning. The 2017 deck set the same destination eight years earlier, with faster numbers.

The report's goal

Indonesia Emas 2045

Indonesia leaves the middle-income trap in 2038–2041 and reaches 2045 as a united, sovereign, advanced, and sustainable state, with the world's fifth-largest economy. Growth of 6–7% a year, led by productivity, pays for change across eight missions.

The 6% path (high income by 2041) and the 7% path (by 2038) are one end-state at two speeds, not two futures. The RPJMN 2025-2029 added a steeper path, rising from 5.3% to 8%, that the law does not contain.

The same destination with faster numbers: high income by 2035 and the fourth-largest economy by 2045. COVID-19 broke its path in the first five years. The 2024 law kept the destination and moved it later (§14).

08 · Where things stand

The directions the plan needs are present; the pace is below its floor

On every rated element, Indonesia is moving in the directions the plan needs, at a slower pace. Manufacturing and exports are up, and the planning cascade holds. Growth and income are below the plan's floor, and the tax ratio has moved the other way. The plan did not model this path.

For a 6% average to 2045, growth now needs 6.1% a year for 2027–2045, above every decade since 1990. For 7%, it needs 7.2% a year. For the RPJMN's 8% in 2029, it needs about 8.1% a year for three years, above any year since 1996.

10 · What has changed since publication

10 challenges and 6 opportunities; two shocks arrived that the plan does not discuss

Twelve changes from one collection run. Each is tied to the claim, path, or goal it bears on, with the mechanism. "In the report?" is a fact about the text. Direction is judged against the vision's own goals. Three changes run both ways and appear in both lists.

Challenges · 10

X2

US tariffs and a bilateral settlement; Western duties on downstream metals

Major shift · Apr 2025 to Feb 2026

Since April 2025, a 19% US tariff, with 0% on 1,819 lines, for near-full Indonesian opening. The EU carbon charge covers stainless steel from January 2026; the US, EU, and UK apply 50% steel duties.

In the report?
Absent
Bears on
Open trade, access from all sides, manufacturing share, no large shock: rules-based access replaced by negotiated terms and duties on the lead products
X10

Middle East conflict and oil shock

Major shift · Feb 2026

Since February 2026, Brent roughly doubled to an April peak. BI's rate rose from 4.75% to 5.5%; the rupiah traded at 17,300–17,900; the World Bank cut 2026 growth to 4.7%. The fuel subsidy is set on USD 70 oil.

In the report?
Absent
Bears on
No large shock, fiscal space, growth: a second dated break; subsidy cost rises with each dollar while the deficit sits at 2.9%

[GAP] "Roughly doubled" from press reports; sources to recover.

X5

New programmes and state vehicles: free meals, Danantara, village cooperatives

Major shift · 2025 · Also an opportunity

Since 2025, free meals have Rp 268–335 trillion for 2026, about 1% of GDP. 82,000 village cooperatives can borrow up to Rp 240 trillion from state banks, serviced from village funds; 10,070 operated by October 2026, against 40,000 targeted.

In the report?
Absent in the law; present in the RPJMN
Bears on
Fiscal space, delivery: budget and capacity committed outside the 20 priority measures
X7

Growth outturn, 2023–2026

Trend · 2023

5.05%, 5.03%, and 5.11% in 2023–2025; about 5.5% in 2026 to Q3.

In the report?
Addressed: the risk the plan is written against
Bears on
Growth, income per head: below both paths
X1

New government; a steeper five-year path, lowered year by year

Major shift · Oct 2024 to Aug 2026 · Also an opportunity

The 2027 target fell from 7.5% to 6%; 8% for 2029 was kept.

In the report?
Continuity addressed; a steeper, then lowered, path absent
Bears on
Growth: lowering the near years raises the pace 2028–2029 must carry
X4

The BPS middle class has shrunk since 2019

Trend · 2019–2025

From 47.9 million to 46.7 million in 2025; about 7.13 million left the class in 2020–2025, while poverty fell to 8.07%.

In the report?
Absent: the plan projects 38% → 80% on another cut-off
Bears on
A growing consuming class: the series the government uses falls while the plan assumes a rise
X9

Second NDC above the plan's emissions path

Major shift · Oct 2025 · Less certain

The 2030 level is 1.35–1.49 Gt, against the plan's 1.03 Gt; the energy sector peaks in 2038; the 2025 renewables target was cut to 17–19%.

In the report?
Net zero by 2060 addressed; the later NDC absent
Bears on
Emissions path: the government's own path sits above the vision's; the basis is still to be checked
X6

Nickel: record exports, one market, state supply management

Trend · 2024–2026

92.6% of nickel exports go to China; the 2026 ore quota was cut by about 25%; prices are low.

In the report?
Mentioned as an achievement; concentration absent
Bears on
Access from all sides, downstream processing: one market does not describe "all sides"
X8

The dependency ratio is rising earlier

Trend · May 2026 · One survey point

45.05 in the 2025 intercensal survey, against 44.02 projected; fertility 2.13; over-65s 11.97%.

In the report?
Addressed: a window of about 15 years
Bears on
Demographic window: it may close earlier unless paths change
X12

The corruption index fell to 34

Trend · 2020–2025

34 in 2025 (rank 109), from a peak of 40 in 2019.

In the report?
Addressed: priority measure 12, indicator 27b
Bears on
Delivery: the plan's own governance indicator moved away from its 2025 value

Opportunities · 6

X11

AI-related goods driving world trade

Trend · 2024–2026

Since 2024, about 15% of world merchandise trade has supplied 42–47% of its growth. Indonesian semiconductor and electronics exports are rising.

In the report?
Absent
Bears on
Open trade: part of why trade exceeds 3.4%. Downstream processing and electronics: no AI-hardware strategy in the roadmap
X3

Generative AI: job effects smaller and differently shaped than "40% of jobs"

Trend · 2022–2026 · Emerging

The ILO puts 3–4% of Indonesian jobs in the highest exposure group and 21.7% exposed; clerical work 93.9%. Jobs in exposed work are still growing.

In the report?
Mentioned in passing: the 40% figure; AI in a list
Bears on
Technological disruption, both ways; productivity: a tool the plan does not name
X2a

EU-Indonesia trade agreement

Major shift · Sep 2025 to Jan 2027 · Emerging

Concluded in September 2025 and sent for signature in June 2026. Entry into force is targeted for January 2027, as EU tariff preferences end.

In the report?
Absent
Bears on
Exports, downstream processing: new access to the EU as US access narrows
X5

Free meals reach; Danantara as one channel for state firms also a challenge

2025

57–63 million meal recipients; state-firm dividends of Rp 142.3 trillion in 2025.

Bears on
Nutrition and poverty measures: no outcome data yet. Finance outside the budget: a new channel, unaudited
X1

The cascade is working also a challenge

2025–2026

The RPJMN, RKP 2026, and RKP 2027 arrived on schedule, quoting the vision.

In the report?
Addressed
Bears on
Continuity: supported
X10

Commodity windfall also a challenge

2026

Higher coal and palm-oil demand in 2026.

Bears on
Fiscal space (revenue), but against the emissions path

Challenges the vision has no measure for

Partner tariffs and negotiated market access (X2). Energy-price shocks and their cost to the budget (X10; priority measure 17 addresses subsidy design, not shocks). A shrinking middle class (X4). An NDC above the plan's own emissions path (X9). Downstream processing that depends on one market (X6).

Opportunities its measures do not use

AI-related goods and generative AI as a productivity tool (X11, X3; priority measure 9 names digital talent, not AI). The EU agreement (X2a; the 2035–2039 "global expansion" phase lists no agreements). Danantara as one channel for state-firm investment (X5). The 2026 commodity windfall, which pulls against the emissions path (X10).

11 · What the report did not cover

The report does not discuss tariffs, a change of government, or new shocks

Topics absent from the law when it was written that have since mattered. Items that are also later changes link to §10.

  • Not discussed: tariff or trade-war scenarios (X2); a change of government as a risk (X1); a pandemic or health shock after COVID-19, or any margin for an outside shock after 2025 (X10); a sovereign wealth or state investment vehicle, and universal programmes with a large recurrent cost (X5; the RPJMN discusses both); generative AI as a distinct force (X3); critical-mineral export limits by other countries (X6).
  • Mentioned in passing: trade, as a 3.4% growth figure and a direction; AI, in a list of technologies (printed p. 104); disruption, as a 40% jobs figure (printed p. 31); financial-sector stress, as fintech risk (printed p. 40).
  • Built in rather than discussed as a risk: continuity, through Mission 8 and the planning cascade.

Part D · The record

14 · What happened to the report

In force since January 2025; the first five-year plan set a steeper growth path
  • Status today. In force as law. UU 59/2024 replaced the RPJPN 2005-2025 (UU 17/2007) from 1 January 2025.
  • What it led to. The RPJMN 2025-2029 (Perpres 12/2025, 10 February 2025) adopts its structure, five targets, and 2025 baselines. It sets a steeper growth path (8% by 2029) and a flatter energy path (renewables 23% by 2029, against 70% by 2045). It adds programmes the law does not contain: free meals, free health checks, food estates, 3 million houses, Danantara as a proposed law, and a state revenue agency. RKP 2026 and RKP 2027 followed; RKP 2027 lowered the 2027 growth target to 6%.
  • Versions. A draft annex (2023-24) came before the law. The enacted annex differs in four places: the vision wording adds "Bersatu" (united); an environmental quality target; a formal-jobs indicator; four environmental sub-indices. It carries one internal inconsistency: the annual emissions baseline is 36.65% in the table and 32.65% in the chart.

The 2017 deck

High income by 2035; 6.5% growth for 2020–2025; industry 32% and investment 39% of GDP; fourth-largest economy; the dependency-ratio low point in 2028–2031.

Visi Indonesia 2045, slides 9–10, 26

The 2024 law

High income by 2038–2041; fifth-largest economy; industry 28%; a smaller investment share, with a productivity story in its place; the dependency-ratio low point "already passed".

UU No. 59 Tahun 2024, Lampiran

The law kept the 2017 destination and moved it later. COVID-19 broke the 2017 path in its first five years.

[TRIAL] Spec v0.2 moves this section up, after §2, for a superseded vision. Here it stays in place, because the main report is in force and the predecessor is paired. Both panels are "then", so neither carries Sky.

15 · How this review was done

AI read the law and gathered evidence; no rating has been reviewed by a person
  • Track. A vision, early-horizon variant: claims tested, change scan in full, goals and commitments listed as "not yet reviewed". The 2017 deck: a superseded vision, reduced review, paired on this page. Chosen because under two years have passed since enactment.
  • What the AI did. Extracted the draft annex, the 2017 deck, and the 2023 keynote. Obtained the enacted law and reconciled it with the draft. Compared the RPJMN's paths with the vision's. Logged 35 claims, 87 goal rows, and 37 commitments, writing "what would challenge it" before gathering evidence. Gathered evidence for three themes, ran the required-rate test on five targets and one change-scan collection, and drafted this page.
  • What people checked. The project owner confirmed four framing decisions (scoring base and law overrides; tracks and pairing; both growth paths in the required-rate test; the BPS middle-class series) and approved each step before the next. No rating has yet been reviewed by a person.
  • Sources used. Official: BPS, Bank Indonesia, Kemenkeu, Bappenas, BPK, KLH; the IMF, World Bank, WTO, APO, and ILO. Research: Mandiri Institute, S&P Global, IESR, Climate Action Tracker, and Transparency International (as an index).
  • Measures we chose. The middle class on the BPS series the RPJMN uses; potential growth inferred from the IMF output gap; the investment-to-growth ratio; the tax ratio as computed from Kemenkeu and BPS figures; the Corruption Perceptions Index, which the law adopts as indicator 27b.
  • Not reviewed. Demography and the consuming class, technology, climate and resources, and regions. 82 goal rows. All 37 commitments for delivery.
